abstracts.abstract: This paper introduces a novel neuro-symbolic knowledge representation framework that fundamentally reconceptualizes how expert systems encode and process domain knowledge. Traditional rule-based reasoning systems suffer from brittleness when encountering scenarios outside their explicit knowledge boundaries, while purely connectionist approaches lack interpretability and formal verification capabilities. Our proposed Hierarchical Neuro-Symbolic Integration (HNSI) framework establishes a bidirectional mapping between neural embeddings and symbolic knowledge representations, enabling seamless integration of statistical pattern recognition with logical inference mechanisms. We formalize the theoretical foundations of this integration through a unified semantic space where neural activations and symbolic expressions are mutually interpretable. The framework introduces adaptive knowledge fusion operators that dynamically weight neural and symbolic contributions based on contextual relevance and uncertainty estimation. We prove the computational properties of our approach, demonstrating that the framework preserves the decidability of symbolic reasoning while gaining the generalization capabilities of neural representations. Experimental validation on benchmark knowledge engineering tasks demonstrates that HNSI achieves 23% improvement in out-of-distribution reasoning accuracy compared to conventional expert system architectures while maintaining full explainability of inference paths. This work establishes a new paradigm for constructing intelligent systems that combine the robustness of data-driven learning with the reliability of formal knowledge representation.

This paper presents an enhanced uncertainty reasoning mechanism for rule-based expert systems that significantly advances the treatment of incomplete and conflicting knowledge in practical applications. Conventional MYCIN-style certainty factor models and Bayesian belief networks face limitations when handling dynamic knowledge bases where evidence arrives incrementally and rules interact in complex ways. We introduce the Evidential Weight Propagation Network (EWPN), a novel theoretical framework that extends Dempster-Shafer theory through a principled approach to belief revision in networked rule structures. The core innovation lies in our computational model for inter-rule conflict resolution, which operates by propagating evidential weights through a dynamically constructed dependency graph. We derive analytical bounds for the computational complexity of our approach, demonstrating that EWPN maintains tractable inference time even for large-scale knowledge bases with thousands of interacting rules. Our theoretical analysis establishes the conditions under which EWPN provides more calibrated uncertainty estimates than existing approaches, particularly in scenarios involving temporal evidence integration. Comparative evaluation across standard decision support benchmarks reveals that EWPN reduces probability calibration error by 18% while requiring 40% less computational overhead than state-of-the-art evidential reasoning methods. This work provides both theoretical rigor and practical utility for building robust uncertainty-aware expert systems.

We present KnowBot, a comprehensive intelligent decision support system that fundamentally reimagines human-expert system interaction through a context-aware multimodal interface architecture. Traditional expert systems typically employ rigid query-response interfaces that fail to adapt to user expertise levels and evolving task requirements. KnowBot introduces a paradigm shift by implementing a conversational reasoning engine that maintains persistent context across extended interaction sessions while dynamically constructing explanations tailored to individual user cognitive models. The system architecture comprises three integrated components: a Natural Language Understanding module that processes free-form queries and extracts semantic representations compatible with the underlying knowledge base; a Contextual Reasoning Engine that maintains session state, manages dialogue flow, and selects appropriate explanation strategies; and an Adaptive Visualization Module that generates dynamic graphical representations of inference chains. We detail the knowledge engineering methodology employed to construct the system's domain knowledge base, including automated ontology alignment and incremental knowledge acquisition from expert interactions. The system was evaluated through a controlled user study involving 120 domain experts across three application areas: medical diagnosis, financial risk assessment, and technical troubleshooting. Results demonstrate that KnowBot achieves 34% improvement in user task completion time and 28% increase in user confidence in system recommendations compared to conventional expert system interfaces, while requiring significantly less training overhead for new users.

This paper describes an enhanced case-based reasoning system with an automated knowledge acquisition pipeline that substantially reduces the expertise bottleneck limiting conventional expert system development. Case-based reasoning systems depend critically on the quality and coverage of their case libraries, yet manual case authoring requires extensive domain expert involvement and remains prohibitively expensive for many applications. Our proposed Semi-Automatic Knowledge Engineering System (SAKES) addresses this limitation through a hybrid approach combining natural language processing of domain documentation with interactive knowledge refinement guided by machine learning. The system architecture incorporates a document analysis module that extracts potential case structures and rule fragments from unstructured text sources, a similarity-based case validation component that identifies conflicting or redundant entries, and a feedback-driven refinement interface that enables efficient expert review of machine-generated knowledge. We implemented SAKES for an industrial equipment diagnostic application and conducted a longitudinal evaluation measuring knowledge acquisition efficiency over six months of deployment. The system achieved a 67% reduction in expert time required for case library development while maintaining diagnostic accuracy within 5% of manually constructed systems. Furthermore, the automated acquisition process identified 340 previously undocumented diagnostic rules from maintenance logs, demonstrating the system's capability to uncover tacit expert knowledge. SAKES provides a practical pathway for rapid expert system deployment in domains where traditional knowledge engineering remains infeasible.
